children: By Isabella Simonetti and Meridith McGraw
President Trump's decision to ban three news outlets from the White House escalated tensions between the president and the journalists who cover him.

After the White House removed CNN from a planned assignment to cover Trump's trip to New York this week, the major television networks collectively agreed to suspend some video coverage of the president. When Trump spoke on the South Lawn on Monday, the White House streamed the event live on its website-but the president's remarks couldn't be heard over the din of a nearby helicopter. Most television networks declined to carry the footage live.

CNN, MS Now and Politico sued on Monday to overturn the president's ban. Trump has rebuffed suggestions that his actions threaten the free press: "The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish," he wrote Monday on Truth Social. "It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America."
Here's how the White House press pool works.
What is the press pool?

The White House press pool is a rotation of reporters, videographers, photographers and technicians who cover the president when he travels or when he conducts events in spaces that are too small for the entire press corps.
The pool typically includes more than a dozen journalists that send written reports, audio, video and photos to thousands of news outlets, who then distribute the information to people worldwide.
How does it typically work?

The television pool, a subset of the broader pool of journalists covering the president, includes ABC News, CBS News, CNN, Fox News and NBC News. The networks take turns serving as the primary television pooler each day. Fox News parent Fox Corp. and The Wall Street Journal's parent News Corp share common ownership.

There is also a separate daily print reporter and a radio reporter, who each distribute reporting on the president's activities to news outlets. Print-pool reports are circulated widely by the White House press office. The Journal is part of the print pool.
A typical pool day at the White House can include covering several events in the Oval Office or other parts of the White House, and last many hours.

For out-of-town trips, whether to Trump's Virginia golf course or to a foreign country, an even smaller group of journalists travels with the president, and goes in Trump's motorcade and on Air Force One. Their job is to report on the president's movements and public statements, and to ask questions on behalf of the entire press corps.
Foreign-pool assignments can last for days. The Journal was the print pooler during Trump's recent weekend trip to Ireland.
Who pays the pool travel expenses?
The cost of the travel is paid by the news organizations.
What is new?

On Monday, the major television networks banded together and suspended the television-pool rotation. They made the move after CNN, which was scheduled to travel Monday to the United Nations General Assembly in New York with the president, was removed from the pool.

The White House is still streaming events live on its website, but viewers couldn't hear Trump's remarks during a Monday event on the South Lawn of the White House because television mics didn't pick up his comments.
On Monday, the New York Times and the Washington Post said they wouldn't publish or distribute still images for the day taken by their photographers who were part of the pool.
The White House launched a new YouTube channel on Monday, called "Trump TV," which it said would stream 24 hours a day and be updated in real time with announcements and "top past moments."
How does this fit into the White House's other media-access actions?

The Trump administration has exercised more control over traditional White House media coverage and introduced other direct-to-consumer options, including a page on the White House website with links to selected articles about his policies, agenda actions and positive polling.

The White House said last year that it would determine which news organizations and reporters can be part of the press pool. It took much of that responsibility over from the White House Correspondents' Association, a nonpartisan media group. The White House also took over the seating chart for the press briefing room, adding a "new media" seat.
